The subsonic aircraft design problem had a takeoff weight of 199,275.6 lb at the optimum solution.
The subsonic aircraft design had four active constraints at the optimum: takeoff field length, excess fuel, maximum pressure ratio, and maximum turbine inlet temperature.
The wave-rotor-topped engine design optimization considered 47 mission points defined by Mach number, altitude, and power setting combinations.
The active design variables for the wave-rotor-topped engine were the wave rotor's rotational speed and heat addition.
The key active constraints for the wave-rotor-topped engine included limits on compressor speeds and temperatures.
The combined COMETBOARDS-NEPP tool produced higher thrust values for the wave-rotor-topped engine compared to the NEPP optimizer alone.
The cascade optimization strategy in COMETBOARDS used multiple optimizers in sequence, with each optimizer starting from the solution of the previous one with some random perturbation.
The cascade strategy allowed COMETBOARDS to converge to the global optimum solutions for both the subsonic aircraft and wave-rotor-topped engine design problems.
COMETBOARDS features that enabled successful optimization include the cascade strategy, variable and constraint formulations, and a global scaling strategy.
The combined COMETBOARDS, FLOPS, and NEPP design tool eliminated the need for manual intervention in the design of aircraft and air-breathing propulsion engines.
The combined design tool was much easier to use compared to the individual analysis tools (FLOPS and NEPP).
COMETBOARDS is written in FORTRAN 77 and is available on Cray, Convex, Iris, and Sun platforms.

The FLOPS analyzer incorporates several disciplines: weight, aerodynamics, engine cycle analysis, propulsion data interpolation, mission performance, takeoff and landing, noise footprint, cost, and program control.
The NEPP code can simulate almost any type of turbine engine configuration and evaluate performance over the flight envelope.
The cascade strategy in COMETBOARDS was able to converge to the same global optimum solution even when starting from different initial design points.
